activity.title: It's been energetic (intended, and very repeated, pun of mine) to see companies like Base Power Company (backed by Ribbit Capital ) and Lunar Energy (backed by DCVC ) turn home batteries into virtual power plants. Interesting subspace here is the software that makes the power worth selling. Found shatterdome energy as part of an #energy intelligence thesis doing exactly that. Looking forward to following the company and congrats to Crucible Capital for leading the pre-seed.

Last quarter I took a remote sensing of the oceans class where I paired NASA's OMI readings with IMF PortWatch daily vessel counts, pre and post the Strait of Hormuz's closure, finding that tropospheric NO₂ fell 34% as a result of the war (worthy of a paper perhaps?). Excited to see this field of satellite-based #energy emissions monitoring grow with startups like Orbio Earth (YC S23) paving the way. OMI: https://lnkd.in/gKkstapx PortWatch: https://portwatch.imf.org/

Having worked at a Y Combinator startup for a year, I'm excited to see so many #energy intelligence companies coming out of the past few batches. With summer at full blast, I petition the next few to have more teams doing what Inviscid AI (YC W26) is doing but for our dorms at Stanford.

Looking back at all of the startups we learned about this year at the Stanford GSB Impact Fund , I'm energized (pun intended) by teams like TrueMeter in helping retailers cut their energy bills. Excited to see them scale as more brick and mortar businesses turn their attention to #energy !

University Climate Ventures hosted dinners for climate tech innovators at Stanford University with SE Ventures and Congruent Ventures to close out the school year! Reflecting on all that we've accomplished in just the past several months has truly opened my eyes to the sheer possibilities that can be achieved in a short time with the right people and the right mission. Since our launch in March, Carolyn He , Sophie Beck , Joe Geniesse , Maahir Gupta , and I have worked relentlessly to build what is now a national innovation platform accelerating climate tech entrepreneurship outcomes for students and researchers at some of the country's leading university technology hubs. With more than 100 innovators and founders in our network, we're proud to have played a small role in multimillion-dollar fundraises, including supporting founders who have been accepted into a16z speedrun and Keel . We've hosted virtual events with packed attendance and in-person gatherings on both coasts, including an incredible investor mixer with the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability Accelerator that brought together a curated group of 30 innovators and investors pushing the frontier of climate technology. This is truly just the start of something special as we work to make climate tech entrepreneurship more accessible, visible, and repeatable across university ecosystems. We believe breakthrough companies emerge when talented innovators have the ecosystem that brings them closer to other founders, investors, and opportunity—and we're building the infrastructure to create this at scale. We're already planning for the next academic year, including new programs for founders and aspiring founders and expansion to several new schools nationwide. A huge thank you to everyone who has believed in this vision, supported our founders, and helped build this community from day one. The momentum is real, and we're just getting started!

Spent the last few weeks at Gigascale Capital heads-down on our photonics theses: photonic compute as the longer-horizon bet, and optical interconnect as a more immediate industry need. I’m increasingly focused on package-level and scale-up interconnect: in-package optical I/O, optical chip-to-chip links, and the enabling layer underneath - modulators, light sources, packaging, substrates, and thermal management. Adjacent to that sit harder system questions around memory bandwidth and capacity, disaggregation, and where optics should enter the architecture. If you’re building, operating, researching, or investing across this stack, I’d love to compare notes and hear what you’ve been working on! All signals welcome. Mike Schroepfer Aaron Bernstein Evaline Tsai, PhD Victoria Beasley Haley Prout Merrill Feather Philipp Hoffmann Olivia Strader Michael Yi Shay Ascher

Last month, I officially graduated from Stanford University with a Master's in Civil and Environmental Engineering, with a focus on sustainable urban systems. Over the past month, I have been reflecting on how much this experience changed me. When I arrived at Stanford, I knew that I wanted to build a career focused on sustainability in infrastructure, but I did not yet know exactly what that could look like. I am leaving with a much clearer understanding of the many ways sustainability can manifest in infrastructure systems, thanks to opportunities to learn by doing, such as: • spending a summer in New York City working with the Built Ecology team at WSP and learning about decarbonization across different scales of the built environment. • travelling to the UK for a week-long Sustainability Changemakers course at the University of Oxford , where I learned how leaders in finance, journalism, policy, and other fields are advancing greener outcomes. • working as a Research Assistant with Dr. Khalid Osman at the Osman Lab, where I studied access to water infrastructure through community-based participatory research. This experience of collaborating with community-based organizations completely changed how I think about infrastructure, showing me that the people using these systems should be at the center of their design. • serving as a Living Lab Fellow at Sustainable Stanford , helping shape Stanford's approach to measuring and reducing embodied carbon by evaluating next-generation tools and informing university policy under the mentorship of Samantha Lubow and David Kirk . It showed me how research, policy, and data can come together to inform real decisions and create impact beyond a single project. More than anything, I am grateful for the professors, mentors, colleagues, and best friends I met at Stanford. They challenged me, supported me, and inspired me every day. Stanford and everything I learned there have changed the way I think about impact, opportunity, and responsibility. I am also excited to share that I joined the Environmental Defense Fund last week as a Lokey Fellow working on clean electricity and markets. I am deeply grateful to Alex DeGolia and the Haas Center For Public Service for making this opportunity possible. This feels like the perfect way to begin my career: working at an organization with a long history of creating meaningful environmental impact and applying the lessons Stanford taught me about combining technical knowledge, policy, collaboration, and public service. I have been incredibly fortunate to have opportunities and privileges that very few receive. I hope to use them responsibly and contribute to a more equitable world with clean air, energy, and water for all.

I came to Canada as a four-year-old. 20 years later, I moved to California to begin my master's. In June, I graduated with an MS in Civil and Environmental Engineering from Stanford University. I won't forget... 1) Working with Clara Medina and Dr. Khalid Osman on community-based participatory research, examining community perspectives on green stormwater infrastructure in Texas, as well as social network analyses during flood events in New Orleans. How can we ensure equity for marginalized groups? 2) Taking hands-on classes in agroecology (and volunteering at the farm!), mycology, and environmental microbiology. 3) Getting to know students from all over the world, seeing how everyone's backgrounds shape who they are today, and what challenges are present in places unfamiliar to me. Now I'm back in Alberta and looking forward to being back at Kerr Wood Leidal Associates Ltd. as a Stormwater EIT :)
